name: Laser hair-growth cap

lead: A laser hair-growth cap is a wearable helmet-style device with an array of low-power red-light laser diodes or LEDs, worn for around 10 to 30 minutes on a set schedule. Several models hold US FDA clearance as devices for treating androgenetic alopecia, and they are sold as drug-free adjuncts to minoxidil or finasteride.

In looksmaxxing communities the caps are discussed as a hands-off way to slow or partly reverse thinning on the crown and hairline. The clinical literature reports a modest gain in hair density rather than full restoration, which is consistent with the dermatology-society position that the devices can help somewhat but do not return a full head of hair.

paras: The approach is called low-level light therapy or photobiomodulation. Red light at roughly 650 nm is absorbed by chromophores in follicle cells, particularly in mitochondria, and is hypothesised to raise cellular energy output, prolong the growth phase of the hair cycle and reduce follicular inflammation. The exact pathway has not been established, and the optimal wavelength, dose and schedule have not been determined.

Side effects are reported as rare and mild, mostly scalp warmth, dryness or tingling. Pooled analyses of sham-controlled trials report an average density gain, but the trials are small, short and often manufacturer-linked, with substantial heterogeneity. Results are reported to depend on consistent use for months, and benefits fade when use stops. Many lower-priced caps sold online are LED-only products with no clinical data, so FDA clearance is specific to individual models. Studies and guidelines generally place the devices below finasteride or minoxidil in effect when used alone.

lead: A laser hair-growth cap is a wearable helmet- or cap-style device containing an array of low-power red-light laser diodes or LEDs, worn for a set number of minutes on a regular schedule to treat thinning hair. It applies low-level laser (light) therapy, also called photobiomodulation, to the scalp and is sold as a drug-free option for androgenetic alopecia (pattern hair loss), alone or alongside minoxidil or finasteride.

Systematic reviews of randomized and clinical trials report that low-level laser therapy improved hair density in androgenetic alopecia compared with sham or baseline. A 2017 meta-analysis in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology found low-level laser therapy superior to placebo in men, with high heterogeneity among studies, and noted that the HairMax LaserComb is FDA-cleared for androgenetic alopecia.[1] A 2016 systematic review of 11 studies (680 patients) found improved hair counts in nine,[2] and a 2018 review of 13 trials reported significant improvement in 10 of 11 trials with statistical analysis.[3]
The reviewers caution that studies are small and heterogeneous, optimal wavelengths and power are not established, and satisfaction gains were less marked than objective ones.[2][3]

paras: Caps hold dozens of laser diodes or LEDs that sit close to the scalp. Typical programs involve sessions of several minutes to half an hour a few times per week, continued for months. Handheld laser combs and bands apply the same principle. The devices are classed as low-level (cold) laser therapy, a modality that uses light below levels that heat tissue.

Grokipedia credits Endre Mester with the discovery of low-level laser effects on tissue in 1967, and describes the technology as photobiomodulation with wavelengths of 600-1000 nm.[4] Hair-growth devices were later cleared by the US FDA as Class II medical devices; the HairMax LaserComb is named among the FDA-cleared products for androgenetic alopecia in a 2017 meta-analysis.[1]

The proposed mechanism is that red or near-infrared light is absorbed in cells by mitochondrial enzymes such as cytochrome c oxidase, increasing cellular energy production and reducing inflammation, which proponents say may prolong the growth phase of hair follicles.[4] The 2018 review states that the mechanism of action and the optimal power and wavelength still need to be established.[3]
Human trials of low-level laser therapy for androgenetic alopecia, including device-based studies, are summarized in several reviews.

A 2017 systematic review and meta-analysis restricted to good- or fair-quality randomized controlled trials compared nonsurgical treatments with placebo. Low-level laser therapy in men, 5 percent and 2 percent minoxidil, and 1 mg finasteride were each superior to placebo. The authors listed high heterogeneity as a limitation and concluded that these treatments were effective for promoting hair growth in men.[1]

A 2016 systematic review of eleven studies covering 680 patients (444 men, 236 women) found statistically significant improvements in hair count or density in nine of eleven studies, improved hair thickness in two of four, and positive but less pronounced patient satisfaction. The authors called the findings promising while advising caution.[2]

A 2018 review identified thirteen clinical trials; ten of eleven with statistical analysis showed significant improvement compared with baseline or controls, two trials showed efficacy in combination with minoxidil and one with finasteride. The authors described the therapy as appearing safe and called for research on optimal power and wavelength.[3]

Reviews describe low-level laser therapy as safe with minimal adverse effects.[3] Reported sensations include scalp warmth, dryness or tingling. Grokipedia lists direct eye exposure and treatment over tumors as contraindications for low-level laser therapy generally.[4]

Laser caps are discussed in hair-loss communities as an adjunct to finasteride and minoxidil. Threads on forums such as Tressless and Hair Loss Talk include users asking whether others have had results with low-level laser therapy,[5] asking for positive reviews of laser caps[6] and asking whether apparent regrowth after months of oral finasteride with a laser cap every other day is real.[7] Experiences posted in such threads are anecdotal.

Products differ in number of diodes, laser versus LED sources, session length and price, and whether the device holds FDA clearance. Reviewers note that studies used varied wavelengths and power levels, so results from one device do not necessarily generalize to another.[3]
